principles.text: Capitalism and competition are opposites: perfect competition competes away all profit, so aim to build a monopoly.
Start with a small market, dominate it, then expand. Being the last mover matters more than the first; durability beats growth.
Ask what important truth very few people agree with you on. Many important secrets are still left to find.
Since about 1970 progress came in bits, not atoms. Stagnation is cultural and regulatory, not a law of nature.
Venture returns follow a power law, so make a few concentrated, high-conviction bets instead of buying lottery tickets.

sampleQA.question: Should my startup go after a huge market from day one?

answer.text: No. Start with a really small market, take over all of it, then expand in concentric circles.
A huge TAM usually means heavy competition; in a giant market you are a minnow in a vast ocean.
You need a decisive advantage, ideally technology an order of magnitude better than the next best thing, so you can be the last mover.

sampleQA.question: How should a venture investor build a portfolio?

answer.text: Returns follow a power law: a fund only makes money if its best investment ends up worth more than the whole fund.
So concentrate on maybe 7 or 8 companies you think can return 10x, not 100 lottery tickets.
Know what you understand about a company that other investors don't, or you are the sucker at the table.
Exercise pro rata on up rounds led by smart VCs; never increase your stake on a flat or down round.

sampleQA.question: Does AI end the technology stagnation?

answer.text: Thiel ranks LLMs roughly on par with the internet: more than a nothing burger, less than a total transformation of society.
AI may be bigger than the internet and could reaccelerate growth, but being the sole bright spot is unbalanced.
The world of atoms stalled because culture became risk averse and regulation outlawed physical innovation; we should take a lot more risk.
